extracted.intended_audience: bibliographers, editors, and literary scholars working on early‑modern English texts and editions
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidentiary examples for bibliographic editing, textual attribution, and assessment of editions and manuscripts of early‑modern 'characters' (essays/character sketches). Emphasises how to determine edition priority, assess manuscript evidence, and judge editorial value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial care, accuracy, and enlargement
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘More care, attention, accuracy and valuable enlargement from an inexhaustible stock of materials has rarely been witnessed than in the editorial labours of Dr. Bliss.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate an edition by the editor’s thoroughness: careful collation, accuracy in text, and the value of added materials (annotations, explanatory matter). High editorial value is signalled by judicious enlargement and correction of the base text rather than prolix or careless additions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Notes should be instructive without prolixity
rubrics_metrics.description: ‘The notes are instructive without prolixity: the index is extremely useful…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor notes that clarify and illuminate the text concisely. Avoid overly long or tangential annotations; usefulness and concision are positive attributes. An effective index complements concise notes by revealing dispersed useful material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appendix value (black-letter and documentary material)
rubrics_metrics.description: The appendix ‘contains an ample store of black-letter information, and will introduce almost every reader to some new acquaintances…’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An edition’s appendices should gather rare or primary-source material (e.g., black-letter texts, documentary extracts) that meaningfully augment readers’ understanding. Such material increases an edition’s scholarly usefulness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve and document title‑page and imprint alterations
rubrics_metrics.description: Noting that a copy had a ‘castrated title and leaf… with the addition of a proof title page with Dr. Bliss's name omitted’ and the alteration of 'Ex dono editoris' to 'impressoris.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Record any alterations, suppressions, or additions on title-pages and imprints (handwritten or printed). These affect provenance, attribution, and bibliographic identification and should be transcribed and explained in the editorial apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use title-pages and imprint statements to determine edition priority
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparison of variant 1628 title-pages (e.g., 'W. Stansby for Edward Blount' vs. 'W. Stansby for Robert Allot') to sort the three 1628 issues and determine their relative priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collate all extant title-pages and imprint statements; differences in wording, printer/publisher names, and layout are prime evidence for establishing edition relationships and priority. Present a reasoned argument when priority is uncertain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collate institutional holdings to reconstruct publication history
rubrics_metrics.description: Tabular comparison showing which institutions (Bliss, Sale, British Museum, Bodleian) hold which issues/editions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Survey major library holdings and sale copies to map edition distribution and survival. Use presence/absence across repositories as evidence for rarity, dating, and variant readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manuscript colophons and handwriting as dating/authenticity evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The Durham MS has a colophon: 'Finis. December This 14th day 1627.' The MS is written in a neat, small hand and contains readings free from some blunders in early printed copies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat explicit colophon dates and paleographic features (hand, ruling, ink) as key evidence for dating manuscripts. Note when cataloguers have misdated manuscripts and document reasons (e.g., colophon vs. later catalogue dates).

rubrics_metrics.name: Document omitted notes and illustrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Explicitly list ‘The notes and illustrations which Dr. Bliss did not make use of in his edition are as follows.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When preparing or assessing an edition, document material known to the editor that was excluded. Listing omitted items helps later editors judge editorial choices and may recover useful textual or contextual data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contemporary testimonies and diaries for authorial biography and reputation
rubrics_metrics.description: Cites Evelyn’s Diary and other contemporaneous hands to support claims about Earle’s life and reputation (dinners, offices, character as ‘excellent scholar’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate evidence from diaries, letters, and memoirs to build authorial biography and reception history. Weigh conflicting accounts and present them with sources so readers can judge reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess literary qualities of character‑sketches (wit, force, liveliness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monthly Review praised the work as ‘a store house of wit and wisdom… The old fashioned dress… adds much to their force and liveliness. The lovers of proverbial wit… are therefore greatly obliged to Mr. Bliss.’
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating character sketches, consider qualities such as wit, proverbial density, and the effect of archaic diction or 'dress' on intelligibility and vivacity; note whether antiquated style enhances or impairs force and liveliness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize shifts in genre (character‑sketch to essay/pamphlet)
rubrics_metrics.description: Observation that 'the essay and the pamphlet gradually usurp the place of social studies' and that later seventeenth‑century characters are often political or religious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Place texts in their evolving genre context: identify when character sketches give way to essays/pamphlets and how that shift affects subject matter, tone, and intended audience. Use genre history to interpret content and editorial approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Catalogue titles and subjects to illustrate class range
rubrics_metrics.description: Long enumerated list of titles and character types (e.g., 'The Coffee-House', 'The Tincker of Torvey', 'The picture of a modern Whig', 'divine characters').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compile comprehensive title lists and subject classifications from copies and notes to demonstrate scope and variety within a literary class; use such lists to contextualize the work among contemporaries and variants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-check bibliographic claims with expert consultation
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledgements to Mr. Madan and Professor Rowley for compiling the table of editions and for authoritative consultation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Validate difficult bibliographic questions (e.g., edition priority, catalog discrepancies) by consulting specialists, sub-librarians, or published catalogs; acknowledge and document expert input in the apparatus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weigh conflicting contemporary evaluations and epithets
rubrics_metrics.description: Contrast between Clarendon's descriptions and other epithets (e.g., 'wary and cultivated' vs. 'negligence in dress'); reconcile these in assessing the author's public persona.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When sources give divergent characterizations of an author, present both and discuss plausible reasons for disparity (genre, audience, political stance). Avoid asserting a single unqualified judgement without noting counter‑evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be alert to typographical, advertorial, and cataloguing anomalies
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted mislabelling in an advertisement (calling the duodecimo an octavo), doubtful dates (a 'very doubtful' 1659), and mistakes in cataloguing the Durham MS as 'about 1636'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat printers' adverts and later catalog entries with skepticism; corroborate physical evidence (format, colophon, paper, type) before accepting stated formats/dates. Flag and discuss anomalies rather than ignoring them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trace translations and influence as part of textual reception
rubrics_metrics.description: Mentions translations/adaptations such as 'Le vice ridicule' (1671) and other works showing Earle's influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document translations, adaptations, and printed reworkings to map a text's reception and influence. Include dates, forms, and how the versions modify or preserve the source.
